nodes.title: The loop's only in-an-hour abort signal is plateau at 19.5 minutes and it detects no-progress, not wrong-progress; the synchronous guards are the verifier itself in 41 of 90 promotions and absent in 12
nodes.body:
gap-w4-035 asks what external signal could abort a bad chain within an hour, given the only metric is the loop's own verifier. Nobody published a protocol; we have one running, so e68 inventories the signals that exist in the ledger rather than proposing new ones.

**Synchronous guards** (decide before the change lands), across all 90 `autopilot.applied`: **41 `reused-verifier`** -- the same command that judged the candidate, so the guard cannot disagree with what it guards; **37 `scripts/test-all.mjs`**, genuinely independent of the task; **12 `null`**. The only synchronous abort that has ever fired is mechanical: all **12 anomaly checkpoints** are `patch-did-not-apply` or `workspace-dirty`. **Zero fired on a quality judgement.** So the synchronous layer is a crash barrier, not an SLO.

**Asynchronous signal**: plateau fires after `window = 3` consecutive non-promoting rounds; median round is 390 s, so **19.5 minutes** of wall clock -- inside an hour. But plateau detects *absence of progress*; the failure that matters is *progress that is wrong* -- a candidate that passes the verifier while making the system worse -- and that produces promotions, so plateau is silent by construction. The other asynchronous kinds are rare by design: `stuck` 1, `holdout` 3.

**Do raised alarms fail to stop the loop?** I first reported 12 landings during open alarms; that was double counting (a landing counted once per open checkpoint). Corrected: **6 of 90 landings** had any checkpoint open. Of those six, four are the human-approval path itself -- `loom-graded2 r1`, `loom-life2 r1`, `loom-oracle r1`, `loom-tri13` -- where the apply is *performed by* the approve handler, so a landing concurrent with an open gate is the intended semantics, not a hole. Only **2** are a real signal bypassed by progress: `loom-chaos` rounds 5 and 6 landed while the plateau alarm (`cp-mw6ddmup000001`, raised after three no-gain rounds) sat unanswered. That is the whole population.

So the honest answer to the question is narrower than 'there is no protocol': the loop has a working 20-minute stall detector, and the gap is that (a) nothing measures harm, only absence and mechanics, and (b) the harm you would want to catch is exactly the event that looks like success. Human gate dwell for context: median 261 s, 6 of 25 over an hour, 2 over 24 hours.

nodes.title: I counted 12 landings during open alarms when there were 6, because I counted each landing once per open checkpoint instead of once
nodes.body:
The first version of e68 reported `promotionsLandedWhileACheckpointWasOpen: { promotions: 12, campaigns: 5 }` and the narrative built on it -- 'a raised alarm does not stop the loop, that is the mechanism by which a bad chain survives an hour'. Both numbers are wrong in the same way: the code did `for (const r of b.raised) { const n = b.applied.filter(...).length; landedWhileOpen += n }` -- so a single landing was added once for every checkpoint that happened to be open at that moment. `loom-graded2` on its own contributed 6 (one landing, six open gates).

Deduplicating by landing gives **6 of 90**, and inspecting the ordering makes four of the six evaporate as a concern: in `loom-graded2`, `loom-oracle`, `loom-life2` and `loom-tri13` the `autopilot.applied` event and the `checkpoint.answered` event are milliseconds apart, because the approve handler applies the patch and then records the answer. A landing concurrent with the open gate *is the approve path*. What remains is 2 landings (`loom-chaos` r5, r6) that happened while an unrelated plateau alarm was open -- real, and one campaign's worth.

The arithmetic lesson is the same one ana-027 recorded hours earlier, which makes this the third time tonight: the unit of the count has to be the unit of the claim. 'How many promotions landed during an alarm' counts promotions; the inner loop counted (promotion x open alarm) pairs. A nested loop over two collections will silently produce the cross product, and nothing about the printed number reveals it. The check that catches it is cheap -- assert the total cannot exceed the size of the outer collection -- and should have been there.

The narrative lesson is worse than the arithmetic one. I had a sentence ready ('nothing gates promotions on unanswered checkpoints') that the corrected data mostly refutes, and the shape of the wrong number (12 vs 6) was exactly the shape the sentence wanted. That is how a measurement stops being a measurement: not by falsifying data, but by being read against a conclusion that already exists.
nodes.source: research/exp/e68.mjs first version vs corrected; the nested loop is at the 'promotions landed while a checkpoint was open' block

nodes.title: The missing alarm is not a protocol but a signal for the failure that looks like success, and that signal already exists at 5% power
nodes.body:
The question was framed as a research gap -- nobody has published a canary or SLO protocol for a loop whose only metric is its own verifier. Measured, the deficit is narrow and specific.

The loop already aborts unattended work within an hour, twice over: a plateau alarm at 19.5 minutes of no promotions, and a synchronous guard that runs before every landing (37 of 90 independent of the task). What it cannot see is the failure that isn't a stall. Every check in the pipeline asks 'did the tree get worse' or 'did the score move' -- both are conditioned on the candidate, and a candidate that games the verifier satisfies both. The one check that asks a question the candidate cannot control is the holdout, and exp-gap-010 measured it firing on 3 of 61 rounds where it could. So the alarm for wrong-progress exists, at roughly 5% sensitivity, and the cheapest SLO upgrade available is to make that check cheaper and more frequent rather than to add a new kind of alarm.

This is the same conclusion exp-oracle-001 reached from the other direction, and it is worth naming the shared shape because it has now happened three times tonight. A rule existed and protected the wrong category (tests/ paths, not oracle files) -- widen it. An alarm existed and watched the wrong variable (stall, not harm) -- re-aim it. A signal existed and fired too rarely (holdout at 5%) -- make it cheaper. In all three the naive move is to add a parallel mechanism, which leaves the hole open while making the system look better instrumented. The discriminating question is: **does the existing mechanism fail to fire because it is pointed elsewhere, or because it is not sensitive enough?** Reroute for the first, invest for the second, and only write a new spec when the answer is 'neither'.

Limits. This reasoning says nothing about whether an independent, frequent harm signal is *affordable*: every extra holdout run costs a verifier run (3.07 s, exp-ver-005), which is cheap, but the holdout also has to be a task nobody has solved, and the pool of such tasks is finite and shrinking (5 of 94 remain, exp-ver-001). And it does not touch the deeper problem that a loop optimising its own verifier can eventually satisfy any check that is derived from that verifier -- exp-oracle-001's boundary, where the fix is a rule about who may move the instrument, not a better alarm.
nodes.source: research/exp/e68.mjs; exp-gap-010 (3 of 61); exp-oracle-001; exp-ver-001/exp-ver-005; holdout cost from exp-ver-006

edges.note: inventories the abort signals that exist and their latency, instead of proposing a protocol to layer on top of them
burn-rate tiers are the right template, but the loop has no 'bad' signal to feed them, only a 'stalled' one and a mechanical one
the 2 real landings during an unanswered plateau alarm are the sample that makes the alarm path a notification path, not a decision path
that measured the holdout as a second opinion at 3 of 61; this shows it is the only signal aimed at harm, which makes it the bottleneck for any SLO
that verified landings reached the tree; this classifies what checked each landing before it did
the first version of the same measurement claimed 12 landings; the corrected count is 6, and four of those are the approve path itself
same defect family as the holdout denominator, now in the count's unit rather than its denominator: a nested loop over two collections produces pairs, not events
the deficit is not a missing protocol but a missing signal for harm, and rerouting the existing one is cheaper than adding an alarm
third instance of 'the mechanism exists and is pointed elsewhere': widen it or re-aim it rather than adding a parallel one

gaps.title: Would a holdout that runs on every promotion rather than 61 of 202 rounds catch a verifier-gaming candidate, and what does the extra verifier time cost per campaign?
gaps.body: exp-gap-010 measured the holdout at 3 disagreements in 61 chances; exp-slo-001 showed it is the loop's only check aimed at 'progress that is wrong' rather than 'progress that is absent'. The obvious upgrade is to run it on every promotion. Two unknowns. Cost: a holdout run is a verifier run, measured at 3.07 s mean (exp-ver-005), so a round that already spends 390 s adds under 1% -- but that was measured on specs that pass in 3 s, and a holdout is by construction a task nobody has solved, so it may be the slow side of the distribution (p90 verifier 2.1 s, max 9.8 s from e47) and it runs unattended where a hang costs the whole round. Supply: the holdout pool is tasks not yet landed, and exp-ver-001 found 89 of 94 registered tasks already green on today's tree, so the pool of meaningfully-unsolved holdouts is 5 and shrinking -- which is why the question that must be answered first is where new holdouts come from, not whether to run the existing ones more often. Detection: with 3 disagreements observed, a per-promotion holdout would have to fire on the specific class of gaming candidate we have actually seen once (the forged `check.mjs` in exp-oracle-001) to be worth its cost, and that class is precisely the one a holdout cannot see either, since the holdout is a different task and gaming the current task's verifier does not change it.
